notes:
I found good material for the traditional verse-by-verse reading and for the popular debate over v. 22. I found nothing from the Catholic, Orthodox, NET Bible or Bible Odyssey sites, and no real disagreement between Protestant traditions in these verses, so those sections are thin or missing. The scholarly debate about where the psalm came from is reported only second-hand, through older commentaries. Labels like "Anglican" are used only where a page gave them.

**v. 1**
- Guzik: after many years, ever since the ark was lost in battle, it is back at the centre of Israel's national life. Burnt offerings stood for consecration (giving oneself wholly to God) and peace offerings for fellowship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/
- Pulpit Commentary: 15:1 says plainly that David had pitched a tent ready for the ark. But the failed first attempt (ch. 13; 2 Sam 6) mentions no tent, and suggests David meant to take the ark into his own home for a while. The two sacrifices speak of atonement and of reconciliation and peace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/16.htm
- Matthew Henry: it was only a tent, a poor dwelling, yet it was the tabernacle David often speaks of fondly in his psalms. "The church's poorest times were its purest." He admits he can't say why David didn't bring the ark to the tabernacle at Gibeon. Perhaps Moses' old curtains were too worn to move. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_chronicles/16.htm
- Ellicott: vv. 1–3 should not have been split off from the end of chapter 15. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/16-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Matthew Henry: David blesses the people "as a father, as a prophet." He notes that the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) reads "in the name of the Word of the Lord." Henry takes that Word to be the eternal Word through whom all blessings come. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_chronicles/16.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: David and Solomon came closer to a fatherly relationship with the people than anyone since the patriarchs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/16.htm
- Pulpit Homiletics: David did not offer the sacrifices himself. What he did through the priests he directed is described as his own act. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_chronicles/16.htm

**v. 3**
- The second food item is uncertain. Guzik quotes Selman: it was either a date cake or a portion of meat, and meat would have been especially generous since ordinary Israelites rarely ate it. Payne: the people ate most of the peace-offering meat "as guests of God's table." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/
- Pulpit Commentary: David was only one channel of God's bounty. The mention of women shows either that they took a recognised part in the festival or that they and their homes were not forgotten. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/16.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: David set up a lasting institution of worship. It was meant to be an ongoing ministry to God, not a one-day high. On "to commemorate" he passes on Spurgeon's advice from the sermon *The Recorders*: keep a journal of God's mercies, praise at once, set aside time to meditate, and talk about God's mercy to others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/
- Pulpit Commentary: the service had three parts. The people were reminded of God's deeds, then gave heartfelt thanks, and finally offered adoring praise, the purest form of worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/16.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: Heman had earlier been named worship leader (15:17), but now David raised Asaph to the role. Payne suggests Asaph's senior clan and his skill as reasons, since Asaph and his descendants are credited with twelve psalms. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/
- Pulpit Commentary: the first "Jeiel" should probably be the Jaaziel of 15:18. Asaph's cymbals kept time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/16.htm

**v. 6**
- Gill: the trumpets sounded continually before the ark, morning and evening. Pulpit Commentary: Jahaziel is probably the Eliezer named with Benaiah in 15:24, or the other way round. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/16-6.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: better translated as David first committed the giving of thanks to Asaph and his brethren. Pulpit: "first" marks the formal start of set public worship in the capital. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/16-7.htm
- Matthew Henry: David wrote the psalm earlier and handed it to Asaph now, for the church's use. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_chronicles/16.htm
- Guzik and Payne: the psalm draws on Psalms 105, 96 and 106. Those psalms have no titles in the Psalter, so David's use of them here suggests he wrote them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/

**vv. 8–10**
- Guzik: the opening sounds like a command, but it is too excited to be one. It invites God's people to join in praise. He counts at least eight ways to praise God here. Some are spoken to God, some to others, and some to oneself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/
- Matthew Henry: we glorify God by our thanks, our prayers ("call on his name"), our songs and our conversation.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/1_chronicles/16.htm
- On v. 10, Henry says those who give glory to God's name may glory in it, valuing their relationship to God and relying on his promise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_016.cfm

**v. 11**
- Matthew Henry: "seek him by the ark of his strength, in which he manifests himself." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_016.cfm
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: the ark is called "his strength" because of the power it showed at the Jordan and Jericho. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-chronicles-16.html
- Ellicott: "his face" means his presence, especially in the sanctuary, and true devotion is the secret of moral strength. Cambridge Bible: changing only the vowel marks would give "and be ye strong." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/16-11.htm

**vv. 12–13**
- Pulpit Commentary: the call to praise now becomes an earnest call to actually seek the Lord and obey him. Psalm 105 reads "Abraham" where v. 13 reads "Israel." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/16.htm
- Guzik: all creation should praise its Creator, but praise is the special duty of God's people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/

**v. 14**
- Guzik: before singing about God's covenant people, David first says God is Lord of all the earth. His authority is not limited to Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/

**v. 15**
- Matthew Henry: Psalm 105:8 says God "will be ever mindful of it." Since God never forgets it, we must not either. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_016.cfm
- Guzik: the psalm fittingly centres on the covenant because it marks the arrival of the *ark of the covenant*.  He traces the covenant theme from Abraham to the New Covenant in Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/
- Pulpit Commentary: vv. 15 and 19 switch to "you" where the psalm has "they," which brings out the reality of this occasion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/16.htm

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: in the KJV the opening words of this verse are a translators' addition and "should be cancelled." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/16-16.htm

**vv. 17–18**
- Guzik: this is the land promise of Genesis 12 and 13. This part of the psalm is mainly teaching, shaping the people's worship rather than praising directly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: God gave the land as a free, sovereign favour. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-chronicles-16.html

**v. 19**
- Keil & Delitzsch: Chronicles reads "when *ye* were" where Psalm 105:12 reads "when *they* were." They argue the harder reading in Chronicles is probably the earlier one.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/16-11.htm

**v. 20**
- Guzik: 2 Samuel leaves this psalm out. The Chronicler, writing after the exile, included it because it praises God for protecting his people while they were outside the land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/

**v. 21**
- Ellicott: this verse originally completed the thought begun in v. 19. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/16-21.htm
- Guzik: Pharaoh did Israel wrong, but in the longer view of God's good purposes David can still truly say God allowed no one to harm them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/

**v. 22: who are the "anointed"?**
- Clarke: usually taken as the patriarchs, who held royal and priestly power and for whom God stepped in (Gen 12:17; 20:3; 31:24). But it may also mean all the Jewish people as God's chosen. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/1-chronicles/16-22.html
- Gill (on Psalm 105:15): the patriarchs were "anointed" though not with literal oil. They were anointed with the Holy Spirit and his gifts, as all true believers are. Barnes: the words are a poetic way of describing God's providence, not a quoted speech. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/psalms/105-15.html
- Guzik: the phrase seems to mean God's people as a whole, not particular individuals. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-16/
- Pulpit Commentary links the titles to Exodus 19:3–6, Israel as a kingdom of priests.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/16.htm

**v. 22: the popular "don't criticise God's servants" teaching**
These verses are not in my original list of teachings to check, but the debate is well known.
- Conrad Mbewe (TGC Africa): the phrase is often used to shield famous preachers from criticism. He calls the fear of harm for speaking out "African traditional religion creeping into the church." He argues it is about harm, especially physical harm, not fair criticism. Samuel rebuked Saul, Nathan rebuked David, and Paul rebuked Peter. https://africa.thegospelcoalition.org/article/touch-not-the-lords-anointed/
- Stephen Braimah (TGC Africa): in the Old Testament the phrase means physical harm. David even rebuked Saul, so the phrase has little to do with verbal criticism. https://africa.thegospelcoalition.org/article/who-is-anointed-by-god-what-does-it-mean/
- Bible Hub Q&A: it gives no immunity from accountability. It also points forward to Christ, the true Anointed One. https://biblehub.com/q/what_does_'touch_not_my_anointed'_mean.htm
- Desiring God (Baptist group): David would not raise his hand against Saul even after Saul became corrupt; God will deal with him. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/how-do-we-know-jesus-is-the-messiah

**Where did the psalm (vv. 8–36) come from?**
- Keil & Delitzsch report that most later scholars think the Chronicler assembled the hymn from Psalms 105, 96 and 106. On this view he rebuilt the festival songs loosely, the way Thucydides and Livy recreated speeches. Keil disagrees. He says nothing in it rules out David as author, and it never refers to the exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/16-11.htm
- Delitzsch, quoted elsewhere, says the compilers "strung together familiar psalms as a sort of mosaic." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/16-22.htm
- Ellicott (labelled Anglican on StudyLight) calls the psalm a composite. At its first "seam" it breaks off Psalm 105's history and starts Psalm 96 at v. 23. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-16.html
- Constable: Israel's worship was meant to lead to the salvation of the nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/16-18.html
